title: Acceleration and describing changing motion
learning_outcomes: Define acceleration using the accepted physics wording.
Calculate acceleration from a change in velocity and a time interval.
Use a chosen positive direction to find the sign and direction of acceleration.
Distinguish negative acceleration from slowing down.
Describe how velocity changes when speed, direction, or both change.
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm01_l01, students know that velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
Students can distinguish speed from velocity and can include direction using words or a sign convention.
Students can describe displacement and velocity as vector quantities and can interpret positive and negative directions.
new_learning: Change in velocity is final velocity minus initial velocity.
Acceleration has the direction of the change in velocity.
Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.
not_yet_taught: Constant-acceleration equations such as v = u + at
Force as the cause of acceleration

mapped_p2_demands: 9702_m17_22_q03_a tests the controlled definition of velocity.
9702_m24_22_q02_a and 9702_w24_23_q01_a test the controlled definition of acceleration.
supporting_p1_demands: Distinguish velocity from speed when identifying acceleration.
Use signed initial and final velocities to determine a change in velocity, including a reversal of direction.
evidence_basis.teaching_extension: Direct acceleration calculations and explanations using velocity and acceleration directions are taught from the controlled formula and syllabus outcome. They are not claimed as direct demands of the three mapped P2 parts.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical definition items and supporting P1 demands. P2 parts directly support exact definition recall; calculations use supporting P1 evidence.

knowledge_boundary: This lesson describes and calculates acceleration from velocity changes. It does not use motion graphs, constant-acceleration equations, forces, free fall, or projectile motion.

blocks.title: The cyclist who speeds up while moving west
body: A cyclist rides west at 3.0 m s^-1. Two seconds later, she rides west at 7.0 m s^-1.
Choose east as positive. Her velocity changes from -3.0 m s^-1 to -7.0 m s^-1.
Prediction: is her acceleration positive or negative, and is she speeding up or slowing down?
The answer feels surprising. She is speeding up, but her acceleration is negative. This lesson explains why both statements are true.

figure.purpose: Make the chosen positive direction and the cyclist's two westward velocity vectors visible before calculating acceleration.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher sketch of one cyclist at two times on a straight road. Show east as positive. Draw westward velocity arrows labelled -3.0 m s^-1 at 0 s and -7.0 m s^-1 at 2.0 s. Use only essential labels.
figure.alt_text: A cyclist has westward velocities of negative 3.0 metres per second and negative 7.0 metres per second two seconds apart.

blocks.title: What has actually changed?
body: Lesson 1 showed that velocity includes speed and direction.
So velocity can change in three ways: speed changes, direction changes, or both change.
Acceleration measures how quickly that velocity change happens. It does not simply mean moving fast.

blocks.title: Acceleration
body: A large velocity change in a short time means a large acceleration.
No velocity change means zero acceleration, even when an object is moving quickly at constant velocity.
Because velocity is a vector, acceleration is also a vector. It has a direction.
blocks.remember: Acceleration describes a velocity change per unit time, not the size of velocity itself.

blocks.title: Calculate acceleration from two velocities

symbols.Delta v: change in velocity, equal to final velocity minus initial velocity
symbols.Delta t: time interval over which the velocity changes

blocks.units: Velocity is measured in m s^-1 and time in s, so acceleration is measured in m s^-2.
body: Always find change in velocity in this order: final velocity minus initial velocity.
Then divide by the time interval.
Keep one positive direction throughout the calculation.

blocks.title: Resolve the cyclist puzzle
body: Take east as positive. Initial velocity = -3.0 m s^-1 and final velocity = -7.0 m s^-1.
change in velocity = final velocity - initial velocity
a = Delta v / Delta t = -4.0 / 2.0 = -2.0 m s^-2
The negative sign means the acceleration is westward. The cyclist is also speeding up because velocity and acceleration point in the same direction.
blocks.remember: A negative acceleration can make an object speed up when its velocity is also negative.

blocks.title: Compare the two arrows
body: Imagine the velocity as an arrow. The cyclist's first arrow points west. Her later arrow also points west but is longer.
The extra piece needed to turn the first arrow into the second points west. That extra piece is the change in velocity.
Acceleration points in the direction of that change. This arrow idea gives the same westward answer as the signed calculation.

figure.purpose: Explain the direction of change in velocity by comparing vector arrows without introducing motion graphs.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn vector comparison. Show a short westward initial velocity arrow, a longer westward final velocity arrow, and the additional westward section labelled change in velocity. Avoid axes and graph styling.
figure.alt_text: A longer westward final velocity arrow differs from the initial arrow by a westward change in velocity.

blocks.title: Slowing down with positive acceleration
body: Now a scooter moves west at 8.0 m s^-1 and slows to 2.0 m s^-1 west in 3.0 s.
With east positive, initial velocity = -8.0 m s^-1 and final velocity = -2.0 m s^-1.
a = +6.0 / 3.0 = +2.0 m s^-2, so the acceleration is eastward.
The scooter slows because velocity points west while acceleration points east.

blocks.title: Why negative does not mean slowing
body: It is natural to read a negative sign as less or slower. That works for some everyday numbers, so the idea feels reasonable.
In one-dimensional motion, the sign usually records direction. It does not by itself say whether speed is increasing or decreasing.
For motion along one straight line, compare directions instead. Velocity and acceleration in the same direction mean speeding up. Opposite directions mean slowing down.
This is why the westward cyclist can have negative acceleration and speed up, while the westward scooter can have positive acceleration and slow down.

figure.purpose: Contrast speeding up and slowing down through relative vector directions.
figure.brief: Two-row hand-drawn comparison. Row 1: velocity and acceleration arrows both west, labelled speeding up. Row 2: velocity west and acceleration east, labelled slowing down. Include a small east-positive key.
figure.alt_text: For straight-line motion, an object speeds up when velocity and acceleration share a direction and slows when they oppose.

blocks.title: A direction reversal changes velocity sharply
body: A ball rolls east at 5.0 m s^-1, hits a cushion and leaves west at 3.0 m s^-1. The contact lasts 0.20 s.
Take east as positive. Initial velocity = +5.0 m s^-1 and final velocity = -3.0 m s^-1.
The acceleration is westward. Using speeds alone would give 3.0 - 5.0 = -2.0 m s^-1 and miss most of the velocity change.

figure.purpose: Show why a reversal requires signed velocities rather than subtracting speed magnitudes.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn ball before and after a cushion. Before: eastward arrow +5.0 m s^-1. After: westward arrow -3.0 m s^-1. Mark contact time 0.20 s and east positive.
figure.alt_text: A ball reverses from 5.0 metres per second east to 3.0 metres per second west in 0.20 seconds.

blocks.title: Turning can produce acceleration at constant speed
body: A toy car rounds a corner while its speed stays at 4.0 m s^-1.
Before the corner, its velocity points north. After the corner, its velocity points east.
The speed is unchanged, but the velocity has changed because its direction changed.
The car therefore accelerated during the turn. We do not need to calculate the value here.

figure.purpose: Show visually that equal speed does not mean equal velocity when direction changes.
figure.brief: Three-frame hand-drawn teacher sequence of a toy car rounding a right-angle corner. Keep each speed label at 4.0 m s^-1. Draw velocity arrows north before the turn, diagonally during the turn and east after the turn. Add a small note: same speed, changing velocity. Do not use graph axes.
figure.alt_text: A toy car keeps the same speed while its velocity arrow turns from north to east around a corner.

blocks.title: The runner whose stopwatch shows the same speed
body: A runner moves around a circular track at a steady 5.0 m s^-1.
At the eastern side of the track, the runner's velocity points north. Half a lap later, the velocity points south.
The stopwatch can show the same speed at both places, but the velocity vectors are different.
The runner is accelerating because direction changes continuously. This is a second way to see that acceleration does not require a change of speed.

figure.purpose: Provide a second, distinct example of acceleration caused only by changing velocity direction.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn overhead sketch of a circular running track. Mark a runner on the east side with a northward velocity arrow labelled 5.0 m s^-1 and on the west side with a southward velocity arrow labelled 5.0 m s^-1. Add the short caption same speed, different velocity. Do not introduce force arrows or circular-motion formulas.
figure.alt_text: A runner has equal speeds but opposite velocity directions at two points on a circular track.

blocks.title: A reliable method
items: Choose and state a positive direction.
Write each velocity with its correct sign.
Find change in velocity as final velocity minus initial velocity.
Divide by the time interval using a = Delta v / Delta t.
Use the sign to state the acceleration direction.
For straight-line motion, compare velocity and acceleration directions to decide whether the object speeds up or slows down.

figure.purpose: Give students a compact straight-line decision rule for connecting velocity and acceleration directions to changing speed.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn two-column decision grid explicitly titled straight-line motion. Show four collinear arrow pairs. Same-direction pairs: velocity east with acceleration east, and velocity west with acceleration west, both labelled speeding up. Opposite-direction pairs: velocity east with acceleration west, and velocity west with acceleration east, both labelled slowing down. Use arrow direction rather than positive and negative signs as the main cue.
figure.alt_text: For straight-line motion, four velocity and acceleration arrow pairs show that matching directions mean speeding up and opposite directions mean slowing down.

blocks.title: Return to the cyclist
body: The cyclist's negative acceleration did not mean she was slowing down. It meant her acceleration pointed in the chosen negative direction, west.
Her velocity also pointed west, so the magnitude of her velocity increased. She sped up.
The useful mental model is now about two vectors. First find how velocity changes. Then compare the directions of velocity and acceleration.

requirements: Use only essential arrows and labels.
Keep the positive-direction key consistent within each figure.
Do not use graph axes because motion graphs are not yet taught.
Do not generate any image assets during this lesson-authoring pass.

concepts_taught: Acceleration describes change of velocity per unit time.
Velocity may change through speed, direction, or both.
Acceleration direction follows the direction of change in velocity.
For straight-line motion, speeding up and slowing down depend on the relative directions of velocity and acceleration.
representations_used: final velocity minus initial velocity calculations
misconceptions_addressed: Negative acceleration always means slowing down.
A constant speed always means zero acceleration.
Change in velocity can be found by subtracting speed magnitudes during a reversal.
skills_students_can_now_use: Calculate acceleration from initial velocity, final velocity and time.
State acceleration direction from a sign convention.
For straight-line motion, decide whether an object speeds up or slows down from velocity and acceleration directions.
Recognise acceleration caused by a direction change.
next_lesson_can_assume: Positive and negative velocity show direction in one-dimensional motion.
Velocity and acceleration may be zero, positive, or negative.
Motion can have constant velocity or changing velocity.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity.
Gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
